chunks: Abu Ali Al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, from Ibn Fazzal, from Abdullah ibn Ibrahim, from Ja'far ibn Ibrahim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

Four (types of people) for whom a supplication is not answered: A man who sits in his house saying, 'O Allah, grant me sustenance,' so it is said to him, 'Did I not command you to seek (it)?' And a man who has a wife, so he supplicates against her, so it is said to him, 'Did I not make her matter to you?'
And a man who had wealth, so he squandered it, so he says, 'O Allah, grant me sustenance,' so it is said to him, 'Did I not command you with moderation? Did I not command you with rectitude?'
Then He said, 'And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stingy, and are between that, standing firm (in balance).'
And a man who had wealth, so he lent it out without clear evidence, so it is said to him, 'Did I not command you with witnessing?'
Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Imran ibn Abu Aasim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) — similar to it.
ai.seo_question: Why is a person's supplication rejected despite their devotion?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi highlights the principle that divine acceptance of du'a is contingent upon human agency and ethical consistency, specifically linking the supplicant's actions to the specific request. It underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on 'preparation of the vessel' for divine grace, noting that laziness, marital discord, financial squandering, or procedural negligence in transactions act as barriers to answered prayers. The reference to 'those who spend not extravagantly nor stingily' connects this practical wisdom to the Quranic ideal of balanced living.
